title: Cinderella (Aschenputtel)

full_text:
The wife of a rich man fell mortally ill. Calling her only daughter to her bedside, she whispered: "Dear child, remain pious and good, and heaven will always protect you; I shall look down upon you from above." Then she closed her eyes in peace.

When winter came, snow covered the mother's grave like a white cloth. When the spring sun melted it, the man took another wife. The stepmother brought two daughters into the house, who were fair of face but vile and black of heart.

They took away the girl's fine clothes, dressed her in an old gray smock, gave her wooden clogs, and forced her into the kitchen. From dawn till dusk, she carried heavy water buckets, lit fires, cooked, and washed. In the evening, having no bed, she had to lie in the hearth ashes, so that she was always dusty and dirty; and therefore they called her Aschenputtel (Cinderella).

When the father went to the fair, he asked the two stepdaughters what gifts he should bring them. The eldest demanded pearls and diamonds; the second wanted fine silks. But Cinderella said: "Father, break off the first twig that strikes against your hat on your way home, and bring it to me."

The father brought her a hazel twig. Cinderella carried it to her mother's grave, planted it in the soil, and wept over it so bitterly that her tears watered the twig. It grew into a magnificent hazel tree. Three times a day, Cinderella went to sit beneath it, weeping and praying; and each time, a gentle white bird flew into the branches, granting whatever wish she whispered from her heart.

The king proclaimed a grand three-day festival, inviting all the maidens in the realm so the prince might choose a bride. The two stepsisters dressed in embroidered velvet, while the cruel stepmother threw a dish of lentils into the hearth ashes, saying: "If you pick these clean in two hours, you may go!"

Cinderella went to the garden door and called:
"You tame pigeons, you turtledoves, and all you birds under heaven,
The good into the pot, the bad into the crop!"

Flocks of white doves swooped down, picking out every good lentil within an hour. But the stepmother laughed mockingly: "You have no dress, you cannot dance, and you would only bring shame upon us!" And she departed with her daughters.

Cinderella ran to her mother's grave beneath the hazel tree and called:
"Shiver and shake, dear little tree,
Throw gold and silver down upon me!"

The white bird threw down a dazzling robe of pure spun gold and silver, and slippers of silk and silver! Cinderella entered the palace, and the prince took her by the hand, dancing with no other maiden all evening. At nightfall, she slipped away like a deer and returned to her ashes.

On the third evening, the bird gave her a dress radiant as the sun, with slippers of solid gold. When she fled the ballroom at midnight, the prince, having coated the palace steps with pitch, found her left golden slipper stuck fast upon the stair!

The prince rode throughout the kingdom: "She alone shall be my bride whose foot fits this golden slipper!" The elder stepsister cut off her toe to force her foot into the slipper, but two white pigeons perched on the hazel tree sang:
"Rook di goo, rook di goo!
There's blood in the shoe!
The shoe is too small,
The true bride is left at the hall!"

The second sister cut off her heel, but the doves sang again of the blood in the shoe.

Then the prince asked: "Have you no other daughter?" The father replied: "Only a stunted kitchen drudge from my first wife."

When Cinderella washed the soot from her hands and face and stepped into the room, the golden slipper slid onto her delicate foot as if molded for it! The prince looked into her eyes and recognized the beautiful maiden who had danced with his heart.

They were wed with grand rejoicings, and the faithful white doves flew down to rest upon Cinderella's shoulders, accompanying the gentle queen through a long life of wisdom and peace.
moral: True goodness and modesty shine through the darkest ashes; patience is crowned with honor.

quiz.question: What is the central moral lesson taught in "Cinderella (Aschenputtel)"?
options: Presence of mind and quiet wisdom triumph over brute strength.
Acting in haste and anger without thinking
Believing rumors and flattery without proof
quiz.hint: Remember the moral lesson of this traditional story.

quiz.question: How do the characters overcome their challenge?
options: Through patience, calm reflection, and wisdom
By shouting loudly and blaming others
By running away from every problem
quiz.hint: Consider the virtues praised in world folklore.

quiz.question: What memorable conclusion does this story teach young readers?
options: Honesty, kindness, and clear thinking lead to peace
quiz.hint: Reflect upon the resolution of the story.
